pedagogy.summary:
- **Age:** 9–11 years

- **Topic:** How We See Objects

- **Standards — UK (DfE Year 6 Science, Light):** use the idea that light travels in straight lines to explain that objects are seen because they give out or reflect light into the eye; explain that we see things because light travels from light sources to our eyes or from light sources to objects and then to our eyes.

- **Standards — US (NGSS 4-PS4-2):** [curriculum wording omitted; reference 4-PS4-2]. (Assessment boundary: does NOT include knowledge of specific colours [curriculum wording omitted; reference 4-PS4-2].)

- **Operational details:** The target model is the one-way light path: source → object → (reflected) → eye. The dominant obstacle is the extramission belief that something travels OUT of the eye to see — an ancient, intuitive and empirically robust misconception that ordinary telling and even reading rarely dislodge (learners assimilate 'light reflects to the eye' into their existing 'I look out and it brightens the object' frame). So elicit first with diagnostics ('My eye', 'Dark room'), then teach REFUTATIONALLY: name the wrong idea and contrast it ('in real life nothing comes out of your eyes — unlike Superman'). Build and draw the full journey with arrowed rays, and use a physical receiver model (string/wool tracing source→object→eye; a webcam or camera obscura as an eye that light ENTERS). Pair it with diffuse reflection — all surfaces, not just shiny ones, scatter light into the eye — so everyday objects qualify as senders. Expect fragility: gains are often short-lived, so revisit and re-test over time rather than treating one lesson as sufficient.

- **Checkpoint:** Tier B (transitional/early-formal). Although the age sits in upper-KS2, the defining demand is conceptual change: the child must abstract an invisible, directional light path and actively overturn a deeply held intuition (eyes reach out / image flies into the eye whole). This is a threshold concept — mastery means correctly modelling and explaining source→object→eye and rejecting any 'out of the eye' arrow, with the understanding holding up on delayed re-testing, not just immediately after teaching.
bestPractices: Elicit the child's existing model first with diagnostic probes (e.g. 'draw how you see this book') before teaching — extramission must be surfaced to be challenged.
Teach refutationally: explicitly name the wrong idea ('nothing comes out of your eyes — you are not Superman') and contrast it with the correct path, rather than only presenting the right answer.
Build and draw the FULL journey with arrowed rays: light source → object → reflected → eye; insist every ray has a direction arrow.
Use a physical 'receiver' model so the eye is visibly something light ENTERS: a webcam or camera obscura, or string/wool tracing the path from source to object to eye.
Connect to diffuse reflection — ALL surfaces (dull as well as shiny) scatter light into the eye — so that everyday non-luminous objects count as senders of light.
Revisit and re-test over weeks: refutational gains on extramission are often short-lived, so one lesson is not enough.
keyRepresentations: Arrowed ray diagram: source → object → (reflected ray) → eye
String or wool physically tracing the light path from lamp to object to eye
Camera obscura or a webcam used as a model 'eye' that light enters to form an image
Three-holes-in-card or a tube lined up so light only reaches the eye along a straight path
commonMisconceptions: Extramission: the eye sends something out (rays/'visual feelers') to see the object.
Light travels both ways — into the eye from luminous things but out of the eye toward non-luminous things.
Seeing just requires light to 'land on' and brighten the object; the reflected-into-the-eye step is missing.
A whole image or picture of the object flies intact into the eye.
Once eyes 'adjust', we can see in complete darkness.
Only shiny surfaces reflect light into the eye, so dull objects are seen by some other means.

learn.summary: For ages 9–11, teach that we see a non-luminous object because light travels from a source to the object, reflects off it, and then enters the eye (source → object → eye, one way only). Light sources such as lamps are seen by light travelling directly from them into the eye. The central obstacle is the intuitive extramission belief that something leaves the eye to 'reach out' and see. Surface this belief first with diagnostic drawing/probes, then teach refutationally — name and reject the wrong idea and build the full arrowed ray path — and connect to diffuse reflection so dull everyday objects count as light senders. Because gains often revert, revisit and re-test over time.

activities.title: Make yourself able to see it: route the light path
feedback: If you drew an arrow out of the eye: in real life nothing comes out of your eyes to see — you are not Superman. An outgoing arrow does nothing; see whether the object actually becomes visible from it.
If the lamp lights the mug but you stop there: lighting the object is not enough. Ask where the light goes next — it must bounce off the mug and travel INTO the eye.
When lamp → mug → reflected ray → eye is complete, the object becomes visible in the model: the reflected light arriving at the eye is what lets you see it.

Lamp off → in the model (or a completely dark room) the mug cannot be seen: with no light to reflect, nothing reaches the eye. In a real dim room you may still see it faintly, because light from other sources still reflects off it.
Dull matt object still visible: dull surfaces scatter light into the eye too, so everyday non-shiny objects are seen the same way.
activities.rationale: Conceptual change on extramission needs the wrong idea to fail visibly rather than simply be contradicted. Having the learner route light and watch an 'out of the eye' arrow do nothing, while the completed source→object→eye chain makes the object spring into view, makes the refutation experiential. An optional live-recolour cue (grey silhouette snapping to full colour when the chain completes) and a lamp-off toggle make the mechanism concrete, and the webcam-style receiver idea and the dull-surface swap come from the misconception review. This is a research-informed proposal, not a tested intervention.
sourceClaims: Extramission and related vision misconceptions: students describe light going from the eye to objects, light going both ways, or an image entering the eye; diagnostics ('My eye', 'Dark room') surface the belief; recommended models include a webcam as an eye that receives light, and reflection from any surface (not just shiny) links to seeing non-luminous objects.
learnerActions: In an on-screen model of a dark scene with a hidden object (e.g. a mug on a table), take on the goal: 'make yourself able to see it.' (In this model the rays you draw control what can be seen; in real life, drawing arrows does not change what you see.)
First try your own intuition: draw an arrow pointing FROM the eye toward the mug, and notice what happens.
Place a movable lamp and draw a light ray from the lamp to the mug; check whether that alone is enough.
Complete the full chain: lamp → mug → reflected arrow → eye, with a direction arrow on every ray.
Toggle the lamp off and describe what happens to the mug and why.
Swap the shiny mug for a dull matt object and check whether it can still be seen; explain why.
activities.intendedInsight: Seeing is not the eye reaching out; it is light arriving AT the eye after bouncing off the object. If no light reaches the object or no reflected light reaches the eye, the object cannot be seen. Shiny surfaces reflect light mostly in one direction, like a mirror, and dull surfaces scatter it in many directions, so both can send light to the eye.

activities.title: Elicit and refute: 'How do you think you can see this book?'
feedback: If you say your eyes send out rays or 'reach' the book: name the idea explicitly — nothing leaves your eyes; that only happens with cartoon superheroes. The eye catches light; it does not send it.
If you draw arrows both ways: keep the incoming ray but remove the outgoing one — the eye contributes no light, it only receives.
If you stop at 'the light lights up the book': ask what happens to that light next — it must reflect from the book into your eye for you to see.
activities.rationale: A Socratic dialogue is useful for surfacing the belief and naming it refutationally before correcting it, which matches the elicit-first guidance. It pairs well with the hands-on routing task; on its own, dialogue surfaces and challenges the belief but does not provide the felt failure of a wrong light path. Research-informed proposal, not a validated intervention.

learnerActions: Before any teaching, draw or describe how you see a nearby object such as a book ('draw how you see this book').
Answer a Socratic optician/vision-scientist persona who asks what you think travels, and in which direction, when you look at the book.
When prompted, decide whether anything leaves your eye, and justify your answer.
Re-draw the path after the discussion, adding a direction arrow to every ray.
activities.intendedInsight: Putting your own theory into words exposes the hidden extramission assumption so it can be named and replaced with the one-way source→object→eye path.

activities.title: Physical receiver model: the eye is something light ENTERS
feedback: If light reaching the model eye makes an image but no image forms when the path is blocked: this shows light must travel into the eye for seeing to happen.
If the holes/tube only let you see along a straight line: this demonstrates light travels in straight lines from object to eye.
Connect back: whatever the surface — lamp, apple, dull mug — the light ends its journey by entering the eye.
activities.rationale: A concrete receiver model makes the abstract, invisible, directional light path tangible and shows the eye receiving rather than emitting light; string/wool makes the straight-line path physical. These media give a different, complementary experience from screen models. Research-informed proposal, not a validated intervention.
sourceClaims: Extramission and related vision misconceptions: students describe light going from the eye to objects, light going both ways, or an image entering the eye; diagnostics ('My eye', 'Dark room') surface the belief; recommended models include a webcam as an eye that receives light, and reflection from any surface (not just shiny) links to seeing non-luminous objects.

Oak Year 6 'Reflected light' teaches the journey of light source→object→eye, recommends explicit teaching of light rays plus demonstrations and diagram practice, and names the misconception that light shines OUT of our eyes.
learnerActions: Use string or wool to physically trace the light path from the lamp to the object and then to the eye position.
Observe a camera obscura or a webcam used as a model 'eye', noticing that an image forms only because light enters it.
Line up three holes in cards (or a tube) so light reaches the eye only along a straight path, and check what happens when one card is shifted out of line.
State in your own words which way the light must be travelling for the image to form.
activities.intendedInsight: Because an image only forms when light goes INTO the model eye (camera/webcam/obscura), the eye must be a receiver of light, not a sender; light also travels in straight lines along the traced path.

activities.title: Predict–observe–explain: block the line of sight
feedback: If you predicted you'd still see it because it's lit: notice you can't. The card blocks the path between the apple and your eye, so in the light model the apple's reflected light can no longer reach your eye. The apple-to-eye leg of the path is essential.
Closing your eyes: the light still reaches the apple, so your eye is not making or needing to send the light — it only catches it.
Pitch-black room: no light means nothing to reflect into your eye, so waiting never lets you see — eyes do not generate sight in true darkness.

Eye like a camera: both form an image from light that enters them; neither sends light out. (Keep to the image-forming comparison; do not extend into retinal or cellular detail, which is outside this topic's scope.)
activities.rationale: A predict–observe–explain test with the line-of-sight card gives a surprising, checkable outcome that targets the 'light stops at the object' and extramission patterns directly, and the darkness probe heads off the 'eyes adjust to see in the dark' error. Refutational diagnostic items are evidence-informed; this remains a proposal, not a validated intervention.
sourceClaims: Extramission and related vision misconceptions: students describe light going from the eye to objects, light going both ways, or an image entering the eye; diagnostics ('My eye', 'Dark room') surface the belief; recommended models include a webcam as an eye that receives light, and reflection from any surface (not just shiny) links to seeing non-luminous objects.
Extramission beliefs are robust against ordinary education; refutational interventions produce gains that often revert, so the idea must be revisited over time.
learnerActions: Look at a brightly lit toy or apple you can clearly see.
Predict: if a card is slid between the object and your eye while the object stays fully lit, will you still see it? Say why before testing.
Slide the card and observe the result.

Explain what this shows: the space between the object and your eye must be clear. Then, using the lamp-off and dark-room evidence as well, explain why scientists say the light travels from the object into your eye.
Answer follow-up probes: does the light still reach the object if you close your eyes? Could you ever see it by waiting in a truly pitch-black room? How is your eye like a camera?
activities.intendedInsight: The object is still fully lit, yet blocking the space between object and eye stops you seeing it, so the path from object to eye must be clear. Put together with the fact that you cannot see anything without a light source (even with your eyes open), this supports the model that light travels FROM the object INTO the eye, and seeing does not 'make' the light.

activities.title: Delayed re-check: sequence, draw, and refute
feedback: Correct sequence should be source first, then object, then eye — the eye is always the final receiver.
If you say something leaves the eye: nothing does; only light arriving at the eye lets you see.
A complete drawing needs the reflected ray from object to eye, not just light landing on the object.
If an earlier correct answer has slipped back to an eye-out arrow, that's not unusual — this idea can revert, so re-teach and re-test.
activities.rationale: A fixed check tests the model rather than building it against a stubborn intuition, so it is used as a companion rather than the main teaching, and especially as the delayed re-test the research calls for because refutational gains often revert. Research-informed proposal, not a validated intervention.
sourceClaims: Extramission beliefs are robust against ordinary education; refutational interventions produce gains that often revert, so the idea must be revisited over time.
learnerActions: Sequence the three steps of the journey into the correct order: source → object → eye.
Answer a refutational check such as 'Does anything leave your eye when you see something?' and justify your choice.
Draw the complete ray path for a new everyday object, with a direction arrow on every ray.
Revisit this check days or weeks later to confirm the idea has held.
activities.intendedInsight: Being able to re-sequence, reject the outgoing-eye arrow, and draw the full path on a delayed test shows the model has genuinely replaced the intuition rather than been temporarily memorised.

constraints: Keep within the standards' assessment boundary: do not teach specific colours reflected/seen, [curriculum wording omitted; reference 4-PS4-2].
Elicit the learner's existing model before teaching; extramission must be surfaced before it can be challenged.

Teach refutationally — name the wrong idea and contrast it with the correct path — rather than only presenting the right answer, because learners otherwise assimilate 'light reflects to the eye' into their existing 'I look out' frame.
Insist every ray carries a direction arrow and that the full chain source → object → (reflected) → eye is completed, not stopped at the object.
Explicitly include diffuse reflection so dull surfaces, not only shiny ones, count as senders of light into the eye.
Expect fragility: gains on extramission are often short-lived, so plan to revisit and re-test over weeks; one lesson is not sufficient.
A fixed sequencing/drawing check mainly assesses the model and should accompany, not replace, the experiential refutation.
The camera/webcam/obscura is a model of the eye as a light receiver; it is an approximation and is not intended to teach retinal or cellular detail.
Physical receiver models (string, obscura, hole-cards) and screen models offer different, complementary experiences; neither is presented here as the only possible route.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research; sources were NOT re-fetched or re-verified. All activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

Two of the four cited sources were marked verified:false in the source row (the Oak National Academy 'Reflected light' page and the Winer/Cottrell extramission-persistence research); treat the persistence-of-gains and specific lesson-design claims with corresponding caution.

The source material contains several catalog-style comparative claims (e.g. that telling/reading cannot dislodge extramission, that 3D 'adds nothing', that static presentation is 'precisely' what research shows learners absorb without change, and that felt failure is a 'sharper corrective than persuasion'). These were softened to narrowly scoped proposals with stated affordances; the exact sources here do not establish such comparative efficacy or necessity.

The research-backed claim is that ordinary education and refutational interventions often revert over time; the stronger phrasing that 'telling and reading rarely dislodge' is retained only as an instructional caution, not as a proven universal law. The summary and feedback were qualified to 'often/can revert' accordingly.
The 'how is your eye like a camera?' probe is a useful image-forming analogy but must not be extended into retinal/cellular mechanism, which is outside the assessment boundary.

The NGSS 4-PS4-2 claim supports the objective/model content rather than the specific teaching-principle rationales in individual activities, so it is reflected in the summary/objective rather than appended as per-activity sourceClaims support.

The Winer/Cottrell persistence claim is scoped to activities about revisiting/delayed re-testing (the POE and delayed-re-check activities); it was not retained on the initial routing activity, whose rationale has no delayed-re-test component.

assess.poeTask: Show a brightly lit toy the child can clearly see. Predict: if I slide a card between the toy and your eye (the toy stays fully lit), will you still see it? Say why before we try. Then slide the card and explain what it proves about the direction light travels.
probeDeeper: If she closes her eyes, does the light still reach the apple? What does that tell you about whether seeing 'makes' the light?
Slide a card between the apple and her eye — the apple is still brightly lit but she can't see it now. Which way must the light have been travelling?
Suppose we sealed every window and turned off every light so the room was truly pitch black — could she ever see the apple by waiting? Why not?
How is your eye like a camera taking a picture?
assess.correctAnswer: Light travels from a source (the lamp or sun) to the apple, reflects (bounces) off the apple, and then travels into her eye. Her eye receives the light — nothing comes out of her eye.

errorPatterns.pattern: Extramission: 'my eyes send something out to the apple so I can see it' — the tell is arrows drawn FROM the eye, or 'I look at it and that's how I see it'
errorPatterns.nextMove: Refutational teaching — name and reject it explicitly ('nothing leaves your eyes, that's only Superman'); build the full source-object-eye path with arrowed rays; model the eye as a receiver (camera / webcam / camera obscura). Revisit repeatedly because the gain reverts.
errorPatterns.distractor: Her eyes send out rays to the apple, and that lets her see it.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Draws or describes rays going from the eye to the object, or a beam that reaches out; treats seeing as the eye doing something active to the object

errorPatterns.pattern: Light stops at the object: 'the light just lights the apple up and then she sees it' — no light needs to travel from apple to eye
errorPatterns.nextMove: Complete the third leg of the path; use the 'block the line of sight' test — slide a card between apple and eye and she can no longer see it, proving light must travel FROM the apple INTO the eye.
errorPatterns.distractor: Light shines on the apple to light it up, and then she just sees it — nothing needs to go from the apple to her eye.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Draws light source to apple but omits the third leg (apple to eye); says lighting the object is enough for sight

errorPatterns.pattern: Two-way seeing: light reaches the apple AND the eye also reaches out — a simultaneous exchange
errorPatterns.nextMove: Refute the outgoing eye-arrow specifically while keeping the correct incoming ray; the eye contributes nothing to the light, it only catches it.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Draws arrows in both directions between eye and object

responseLevels.gap: Describes or draws light (or 'looking') coming OUT of the eye, or says she sees the apple simply because it is lit, with no light entering the eye.
responseLevels.full: Traces the complete one-way path source-object-eye with the eye as receiver, AND transfers it: explains why the card in the line of sight blocks vision and why total darkness prevents sight, both from 'light must reflect into the eye'.
responseLevels.partial: Names the pieces — light source, apple, eye — and knows light must be present, but leaves the path incomplete or cannot commit to a direction (e.g. lights the object but omits apple-to-eye, or still says the eye 'looks at' it).

assess.diagnosticPrompt: A girl is looking at an apple sitting on a table in a well-lit room. Explain what has to happen with the light for her to see the apple — trace the light's journey from start to finish.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child holding the intuitive extramission model describes or draws something leaving the eye and going TO the apple (or a two-way 'looking' beam); the correct model has light going one way only, source to object to eye, with the eye as a pure receiver. Asking for the direction of the journey forces the mechanism out into the open, where telling and even reading the right answer usually fail to.
